cards.q: Why can the nucleons in a nucleus be treated, as a first approximation, as independent particles moving in single-particle orbits?
cards.a: The nucleon-nucleon force has an almost infinitely repulsive core at very short distances, so nucleons are rarely close enough to experience the strongest part of the interaction. Since they are, on average, relatively far apart, they mostly feel the weaker attractive tail of the force, making independent-particle motion a useful first approximation.

cards.q: The nucleon-nucleon force has an almost infinitely repulsive core at a radius of about $$c\approx0.4\,\mathrm{fm}$$, while the nuclear radius is of order $$R\approx r_0A^{1/3}$$. Why does this make strong nucleon-nucleon collisions relatively rare?
cards.a: The volume occupied by closely packed nucleons is only about one hundredth of the actual nuclear volume. Most of the time the nucleons are therefore far enough apart that they do not probe the strongly repulsive core of the interaction.

cards.q: What is the significance of the mean free path of a nucleon being at least of the order of the nuclear dimension?
cards.a: A nucleon can travel across a substantial fraction of the nucleus before suffering a strong collision. This provides experimental support for the picture of relatively unperturbed single-particle motion inside the nucleus.

cards.q: Once independent-particle motion is assumed, what kind of potential is expected to govern the motion of an individual nucleon?
cards.a: Each nucleon moves in an average potential generated by all the nucleons in the nucleus. The potential is relatively force-free in the interior and becomes confining near the nuclear surface, where the nucleon is prevented from escaping.

cards.q: What are the nuclear magic numbers identified experimentally?
cards.a: The magic numbers are $$2,\ 8,\ 20,\ 28,\ 50,\ 82,\ 126.$$ At these proton or neutron numbers, nuclei show effects analogous to closed electron shells in atoms.

cards.q: The single-particle separation energy is the energy required to remove the least-bound nucleon from a nucleus. What does a large separation energy tell us physically?
cards.a: A large separation energy means that the least-bound nucleon is still strongly bound to the nucleus, so the nucleus is particularly stable against particle removal.

cards.q: How does the nucleon separation energy behave near magic numbers, and what does this reveal?
cards.a: The separation energy shows pronounced anomalies at the magic numbers and is especially large for doubly magic nuclei. This indicates that closed proton or neutron shells provide an additional degree of stability.

cards.q: Why are magic and doubly magic nuclei exceptionally strongly bound?
cards.a: Their proton or neutron single-particle shells are closed. Removing a nucleon then requires overcoming a relatively large energy gap to the next available configuration, giving enhanced stability compared with neighboring nuclei.

cards.q: Why does the excitation energy of the first $$2^+$$ state become especially large near magic numbers?
cards.a: Near a shell closure, promoting nucleons to produce a collective excitation requires crossing a larger single-particle energy gap. The nucleus is therefore more resistant to low-energy excitation, producing a pronounced increase in the first $$2^+$$ excitation energy.

cards.q: Why do the magic-number effects provide strong evidence for a shell structure of the nucleus?
cards.a: The enhanced separation energies and strong stability at specific proton and neutron numbers cannot be explained by a smooth average-density picture alone. They indicate that nucleons occupy discrete groups of single-particle levels, analogous to electron shells in atoms.

cards.q: Why is an average one-body potential introduced in the shell model?
cards.a: If the nucleons move approximately independently, their mutual interactions can be represented indirectly by an average potential generated by all the nucleons. The shell model then treats each nucleon as moving independently in this common mean field.

cards.q: Why is there no net force on a nucleon near the center of a spherical nucleus?
cards.a: A nucleon near the center feels the nuclear attraction from the surrounding nucleons approximately uniformly in all directions, so the contributions largely cancel. Therefore the average potential is approximately flat in the nuclear interior.

cards.q: What happens to the average nuclear potential as a nucleon approaches the nuclear surface?
cards.a: The nuclear binding force becomes weaker toward the surface, so the potential rises from its approximately constant interior value and approaches zero outside the nucleus. This produces a confining potential well for the nucleons.

cards.q: The Woods-Saxon potential is written as $$V^{\mathrm{WS}}(r)=-V_0\left[1+\exp\left(\frac{r-R_0}{a}\right)\right]^{-1}.$$ What physical features of the nuclear mean field does this form describe?
cards.a: It represents an approximately constant attractive potential in the nuclear interior, a smooth transition through the nuclear surface, and a potential that approaches zero outside the nucleus. The parameter $R_0$ sets the nuclear size, $V_0$ the depth, and $a$ the surface diffuseness.

cards.q: Why are the harmonic oscillator and square-well potentials useful approximations to the Woods-Saxon potential?
cards.a: The Woods-Saxon potential does not generally give simple analytic eigenfunctions. The harmonic oscillator and square well are simpler limiting potentials whose solutions can be obtained explicitly and therefore provide useful qualitative descriptions and calculational approximations.

cards.q: For the spherical harmonic oscillator, the energy levels are $$\epsilon_N=\hbar\omega_0\left(N+\frac32\right)-V_0.$$ What is the physical significance of the oscillator quantum number $N$?
cards.a: $N$ labels an oscillator shell, so all single-particle states with the same $N$ belong to the same oscillator shell. The harmonic oscillator therefore groups single-particle states into shells separated by approximately $\hbar\omega_0$.

cards.q: The harmonic-oscillator shell has degeneracy $$D(N)=\frac12(N+1)(N+2).$$ What does this degeneracy mean physically?
cards.a: There are $D(N)$ distinct spatial single-particle states with the same oscillator quantum number $N$. Including the nucleon's spin and isospin degrees of freedom gives the corresponding capacity for protons and neutrons in the shell.

cards.q: Why does a single harmonic-oscillator shell contain states with only one parity?
cards.a: The oscillator shell satisfies $$N=2(n-1)+l$$. Therefore $l$ has the same parity as $N$, and since the parity of a single-particle state is $(-1)^l$, all states in a given oscillator shell have the same parity.

cards.q: Why are different $(n,l)$ states within the same harmonic-oscillator shell degenerate?
cards.a: The harmonic-oscillator energy depends only on the total oscillator quantum number $N$, not separately on $n$ and $l$. This creates an accidental degeneracy between different orbital angular momenta within the same shell.

cards.q: Why do the simple harmonic-oscillator and square-well potentials reproduce the magic numbers $2$, $8$, and $20$?
cards.a: Their single-particle levels form oscillator shells with the appropriate degeneracies. Filling these shells according to the Pauli principle produces closed-shell configurations at $2$, $8$, and $20$ nucleons.

cards.q: Why can the simple harmonic-oscillator and square-well models not explain the higher magic numbers $28$, $50$, $82$, and $126$?
cards.a: Their single-particle level ordering and degeneracies do not produce the required large shell gaps at the higher magic numbers. A more realistic average potential, together with additional ingredients, is therefore needed to reproduce the full sequence of observed shell closures.

cards.q: The plot below shows deviations of measured nuclear masses from their smooth mean values as functions of proton and neutron number. What does the pronounced structure in these deviations tell us?
cards.a: The smooth liquid-drop contribution does not account for all nuclear binding. The systematic deviations reflect shell effects, with pronounced changes near closed proton and neutron shells. This is evidence that the single-particle level structure produces additional microscopic binding.

cards.q: The figure below compares the single-particle levels of an isotropic harmonic oscillator with those of an infinite square well. What is the main physical lesson of this comparison?
cards.a: Both simple potentials generate shell structures and reproduce the low-lying magic numbers $2$, $8$, and $20$, but they produce different detailed single-particle level orderings. The comparison shows that the shell structure depends on the form of the average nuclear potential.
